source_text: Φησὶ δὲ πολλοὺς ἂν καὶ ἄλλους φανῆναι τοιούτους τοῖς ἐξαπατᾶσθαι θέλουσιν, ὁποῖος ἦν ὁ Ἰησοῦς. μὴ πολλοὺς οὖν ἀλλὰ μηδ᾿ ὀλίγους ἀλλὰ κἂν ἕνα δεικνύτω ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος τοιοῦτον, ὁποῖος ἦν ὁ Ἰησοῦς, λόγον καὶ δόγματα μετὰ τῆς ἐν αὐτῷ δυνάμεως βιωφελῆ ἐπεισάγοντα τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ ἐπιστρέφοντα ἀπὸ χύσεως ἁμαρτημάτων. φησὶ δὲ τοῦτο ἔγκλημα ἀπὸ τῶν εἰς τὸν Χριστὸν πιστευόντων προσάγεσθαι Ἰουδαίοις, ἐπεὶ μὴ πεπιστεύκασιν ὡς εἰς θεὸν τὸν Ἰησοῦν· καὶ περὶ τούτου δὲ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω προαπελογησάμεθα, δεικνύντες ἅμα, πῶς μὲν αὐτὸν θεὸν νοοῦμεν, κατὰ τί δὲ ἄνθρωπον λέγομεν. πῶς δὲ, φησὶν, ἡμεῖς οἱ πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις δηλώσαντες ἥξειν ἀπὸ θεοῦ τὸν κολάσοντα τοὺς ἀδίκους ἐλθόντα ἠτιμάζομεν; πρὸς τοῦτο δὲ ἀπολογήσασθαι πάνυ εὔηθες ὂν οὐ δοκεῖ μοι εἶναι εὔλογον. ὡς εἰ καὶ ἄλλος τις ἔλεγε· πῶς ἂν ἡμεῖς οἱ διδάξαντες σωφρονεῖν ἀκόλαστον ἄν τι ἐποιήσαμεν, ἢ περὶ δικαιοσύνης πρεσβεύοντες ἠδικήσαμεν; ὡς γὰρ ἐκεῖνα ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὑρίσκεται, οὕτως φάσκοντας προφήταις πεπιστευκέναι, λέγουσι περὶ ἐπιδημήσοντος Χριστοῦ, ἠπιστηκέναι τῷ ἐληλυθότι κατὰ τὰ προφητευόμενα ἀνθρώπινον ἦν. εἰ δὲ δεῖ προσθεῖναι καὶ ἄλλην αἰτίαν, φήσομεν ὅτι καὶ τοῦτ᾿ αὐτὸ προεῖπον οἱ προφῆται. σαφῶς γοῦν Ἡσαΐας λέγει· „ἀκοῇ ἀκούσετε καὶ οὐ μὴ συνῆτε, καὶ βλέποντες βλέψετε καὶ οὐ μὴ ἴδητε. ἐπαχύνθη γὰρ ἡ καρδία τοῦ λαοῦ τούτου“ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. καὶ λεγέτωσαν ἡμῖν, τί ἀκούουσι [τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις] καὶ τί βλέπουσι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις προφητεύεται μὴ συνήσειν τὰ λεγόμενα καὶ μὴ ὃν δεῖ τρόπον ὄψεσθαι τὸ ὁραθέν. ἀλλὰ μὴν δῆλον ὅτι ἰδόντες τὸν Ἰησοῦν οὐκ εἶδον ὅστις ἦν, καὶ ἀκούοντες αὐτοῦ οὐ συνῆκαν ἐκ τῶν λεγομένων τὴν ἐν αὐτῷ θειότητα, μεταβιβάζουσαν τὴν ἐπὶ Ἰουδαίους τοῦ θεοῦ ἐπισκοπὴν ἐπὶ τοὺς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸν πιστεύοντας. ἔστιν οὖν ἰδεῖν μετὰ τὴν Ἰησοῦ ἐπιδημίαν Ἰουδαίους καταλελειμμένους πάντῃ καὶ μηδὲν ἔχοντας τῶν πάλαι νομιζομένων αὐτοῖς εἶναι σεμνῶν ἀλλὰ καὶ μηδὲν σημεῖον τοῦ εἶναί τινα θειότητα παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς. οὐκ ἔτι γὰρ προφῆται οὐδὲ τεράστια, ὧν κἂν ἴχνη ἐπὶ ποσὸν παρὰ Χριστιανοῖς εὑρίσκεται, καί τινα γὲ „μείζονα“· καὶ εἰ πιστοί ἐσμεν λέγοντες, καὶ ἡμεῖς ἑωράκαμεν. λέγει δ᾿ ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος· διὰ τί ἠτιμάζομεν ὃν προεκηρύσσομεν; ἢ ἴνα πλέον τῶν ἄλλων κολασθῶμεν; καὶ πρὸς τοῦτο δ᾿ ἔστιν εἰπεῖν ὅτι πλέον τῶν ἄλλων Ἰουδαῖοι διὰ τὴν εἰς Ἰησοῦν ἀπιστίαν καὶ ὅσα ἄλλα αὐτῷ ἐνύβρισαν οὐ μόνον κατὰ τὴν πεπιστευμένην κρίσιν πείσονται ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ ἤδη πεπόνθασι. ποῖον γὰρ ἔθνος πεφυγάδευται ἀπὸ τῆς ἰδίας μητροπόλεως καὶ τοῦ οἰκείου τόπου τῇ πατρίῳ θρησκείᾳ ἢ μόνοι Ἰουδαῖοι; τοῦτο δὲ πεπόνθασιν ὡς ἀγεννέστατοι, εἰ καὶ πολλὰ ἥμαρτον, δι᾿ οὐδὲν οὕτως ἐκείνων. ὡς διὰ τὰ κατὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἡμῶν τετολμημένα.
pass_a_gloss: He says that many others too would have appeared such (τοιούτους) to those wishing to be deceived (ἐξαπατᾶσθαι), of the kind Jesus was. Not many, then, nor even few, but even one let the Jew in Celsus show such as Jesus was, introducing (ἐπεισάγοντα) to the race of men, with the power (δύναμις) in him, a word/teaching (λόγος) and doctrines (δόγματα) useful for life (βιωφελῆ), and turning [them] (ἐπιστρέφοντα) from the outpouring/flood (χύσις) of sins (ἁμαρτήματα). He says this charge (ἔγκλημα) is brought against the Jews by those believing in Christ, since they have not believed in Jesus as God; and about this too we defended beforehand in the things above, showing at once how we conceive (νοοῦμεν) him God, and in what respect (κατὰ τί) we call him man. 'How', he says, 'did we, who made clear (δηλώσαντες) to all men that from God will come the one who will punish (κολάσοντα) the unrighteous, dishonour (ἠτιμάζομεν) him having come?' To defend against this, being quite silly (εὔηθες), does not seem to me reasonable (εὔλογον). As if someone else said: 'How would we who taught (διδάξαντες) to be self-controlled (σωφρονεῖν) have done something licentious (ἀκόλαστον), or, acting as ambassadors for justice (πρεσβεύοντες περὶ δικαιοσύνης), done wrong (ἠδικήσαμεν)?' For as those things are found among men, so for those claiming to have believed the prophets, speaking about Christ who would sojourn (ἐπιδημήσοντος), to have disbelieved (ἠπιστηκέναι) the one who came according to the things prophesied was human (ἀνθρώπινον). And if one must add another cause (αἰτία), we will say that the prophets foretold (προεῖπον) this very thing. Clearly, at least, Isaiah says: 'With hearing you will hear and not understand (συνῆτε), and seeing you will see and not see; for the heart of this people was thickened (ἐπαχύνθη)' and the following. And let them tell us what, to the Jews hearing and seeing, is prophesied: not to understand the things said and not to see in the way necessary (ὃν δεῖ τρόπον) the thing seen. But indeed it is clear that having seen Jesus they did not see who he was, and hearing him they did not understand from the things said the divinity (θειότης) in him, transferring (μεταβιβάζουσαν) God's oversight/visitation (ἐπισκοπή) over the Jews onto those from the nations believing on him. One can see, then, after Jesus's sojourn (ἐπιδημία) the Jews left behind/forsaken (καταλελειμμένους) altogether, and having nothing of the things anciently held by them to be venerable (σεμνά), but also no sign (σημεῖον) of there being some divinity among them. For no longer prophets nor wonders (τεράστια), of which even traces (ἴχνη) to some extent (ἐπὶ ποσόν) are found among Christians, and some even 'greater'; and if we are trustworthy (πιστοί) in saying [it], we too have seen. The Jew in Celsus says: 'Why did we dishonour the one we proclaimed beforehand (προεκηρύσσομεν)? Or so that we might be punished more than the others?' To this too one can say that more than the others the Jews, because of the unbelief (ἀπιστία) toward Jesus and whatever else they outraged (ἐνύβρισαν) him, not only will suffer according to the believed judgment (πεπιστευμένη κρίσις) but indeed have already suffered. For what nation has been made exile (πεφυγάδευται) from its own mother-city (μητρόπολις) and its proper place for its ancestral worship (πάτριος θρησκεία) except the Jews alone? This they have suffered as most ignoble (ἀγεννέστατοι), even if they sinned much, for none of those so much as for the things dared (τετολμημένα) against our Jesus.
pass_b_english: He says that many others of the same kind as Jesus could also appear to those who wish to be deceived. Then let Celsus’s Jew show not many, nor even a few, but even one such as Jesus was: one who, with the power that was in him, brought into the human race a teaching and doctrines that benefit life, and turned people from the flood of sins.

He says that those who believe in Christ bring this charge against the Jews, that they have not believed in Jesus as God. On this point too we have already made our defence above, showing at the same time in what way we understand him to be God, and in what respect we call him man.

“And how,” he says, “could we, who declared to all people that one would come from God to punish the unrighteous, have dishonoured him when he came?” To make a defence against this, since it is so very silly, does not seem reasonable to me. It is as if someone else were to say: “How could we, who taught self-control, have done anything licentious? Or how could we, who champion justice, have done wrong?” For as such things are found among human beings, so it was a human thing that those who claimed to have believed the prophets when they spoke of the Christ who was to come should have disbelieved him when he came in accordance with what was prophesied. And if another reason must be added, we will say that the prophets foretold this very thing as well. Isaiah, at any rate, says plainly: “Hearing you will hear and will not understand, and seeing you will see and will not perceive; for the heart of this people has grown dull” (Isaiah 6:9–10), and what follows.

Let them tell us what it is that the Jews hear and what they see, when it is prophesied of them that they will not understand what is spoken and will not see in the way they ought what is seen. Yet it is plain that when they saw Jesus they did not see who he was, and when they heard him they did not grasp from his words the divinity in him, which was transferring God’s care from the Jews to those from the Gentiles who believe in him. So one can see that after the coming of Jesus the Jews have been wholly abandoned, and have nothing of what they once held sacred, nor even any sign that some divinity is among them. For there are no longer prophets or wonders among them, though traces of these are found to some extent among Christians, and some of them even “greater” (John 14:12); and if we are to be believed when we say so, we too have seen them.

Celsus’s Jew says: “Why would we have dishonoured the one whom we proclaimed beforehand? Was it so that we might be punished more than others?” To this too one can say that, because of their unbelief toward Jesus and all the other outrages they committed against him, the Jews will not only suffer more than others at the judgment in which we believe, but have already suffered. For what nation has been banished from its own mother city and from the place proper to its ancestral worship, except the Jews alone? And they have suffered this as the most ignoble of men; for though they sinned in many things, they suffered it for none of those so much as for what they dared against our Jesus.

choices.why: 'many others like Jesus would also have appeared' -> 'many others of the same kind as Jesus could also appear' (ἂν φανῆναι, potential; τοιούτους ... ὁποῖος).
Removed added 'us' from 'let Celsus's Jew show us' (δεικνύτω has no object).
'which moved God's care' -> 'which was transferring God's care' (present participle μεταβιβάζουσαν).
'what they long held sacred' -> 'what they once held sacred' (πάλαι).
'Why should we dishonour' -> 'Why would we have dishonoured' (imperfect ἠτιμάζομεν, matching the Jew's earlier question).
Isaiah 6:9-10 LXX and John 14:12 checked; Celsus/Jew direct and indirect speech kept distinct; the hypothetical speaker remains Origen's comparison.

translator_notes: The first two reports of Celsus’s Jew are indirect speech (φησί + infinitive) and are left unquoted; the two direct questions in the first person plural are in quotation marks. The hypothetical speaker (‘as if someone else were to say’) is Origen’s comparison, not Celsus. Isaiah 6:9-10 agrees with the LXX (ἀκοῇ ἀκούσετε ... ἐπαχύνθη γὰρ ἡ καρδία τοῦ λαοῦ τούτου); also quoted in Matthew 13:14-15 and Acts 28:26-27, but Origen names Isaiah. ‘Greater’ (μείζονα) alludes to John 14:12 (μείζονα τούτων ποιήσει). τί ἀκούουσι [τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις] καὶ τί βλέπουσι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις: Koetschau brackets the first τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις as a doubling; the clause is compressed and τί could also mean ‘why’; ‘what’ is chosen because the next sentence answers with what they saw and heard, namely Jesus. ἐπισκοπή rendered ‘care’ (God’s oversight or visitation). ὡς ἀγεννέστατοι is harsh and slightly awkward in the Greek; translated as printed. The full stop printed before ὡς διὰ τὰ κατὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ is treated as a comma. ‘Banished from its mother city’ refers to the expulsion of the Jews from Jerusalem after the revolts of 70 and 135; Origen’s polemic is translated as written, without softening. πολλοὺς ἂν ... φανῆναι τοιούτους: ἄν with the aorist infinitive in reported speech is taken as potential (‘could appear’), and τοιούτους ... ὁποῖος ἦν ὁ Ἰησοῦς as ‘of the same kind as Jesus’. ἠτιμάζομεν in the Jew’s two questions is rendered as a past unreal question (‘would we have dishonoured’). μεταβιβάζουσαν is present (‘was transferring’); πάλαι is ‘once, of old’.
